summary: This document gives guidelines for personal interaction in the Internet Engineering Task Force. They recognize the diversity of participants, emphasize mutual respect, and stress the broad applicability of IETF work. It updates earlier conduct guidelines.

plainLanguage.summary: The IETF writes Internet standards through group discussion, and the people taking part have very different backgrounds and communication styles. RFC 7154 sets out how they are expected to treat each other. It replaces RFC 3184, the earlier version of the same guidelines.

subtitle: Four rules for how the people who write Internet standards treat each other while they write them.

tldr.problem: IETF work depends on cooperation among a diverse range of people with different ideas and communication styles, and it needs shared expectations for how they treat each other.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out four guidelines: extend respect and courtesy, keep discussions impersonal, devise solutions for the global Internet, and come prepared to contribute.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 3184 as BCP 54 and adds text saying the IETF strives to treat every person with dignity, decency and respect.

facts.label: Report transgressions to
facts.value: The IETF Chair or the IESG

today: RFC 7154 is a Best Current Practice published in March 2014. It obsoletes RFC 3184, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text describes the guidelines and points to other documents for the measures available against a participant who breaks them.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The work of the IETF relies on cooperation among a diverse range of people with different ideas and communication styles. The IETF strives, through these guidelines for conduct, to create and maintain an environment in which every person is treated with dignity, decency, and respect.

People who participate in the IETF are expected to behave in a professional manner as the group works together to develop interoperable technologies for the Internet. The guidelines are meant to be followed as the group builds consensus in person and through email discussions. If conflicts arise, they are resolved according to the procedures outlined in RFC 2026.

This document obsoletes RFC 3184, which held the earlier version of the guidelines for conduct.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF writes Internet standards through group discussion, and the people taking part have very different backgrounds and communication styles. RFC 7154 sets out how they are expected to treat each other. It replaces RFC 3184, the earlier version of the same guidelines.

sections.title: The Four Guidelines
sections.content:
Guideline 1 is that IETF participants extend respect and courtesy to their colleagues at all times. Participants come from diverse origins and backgrounds and can hold different expectations, but they treat colleagues with respect as persons, especially when it is difficult to agree with them: treat other participants as you would like to be treated.

The same guideline says that English is the de facto language of the IETF, but it is not the native language of many participants. All participants, particularly those with English as a first language, attempt to accommodate the needs of other participants by communicating clearly, including speaking slowly and limiting the use of slang. Faced with English that is difficult to understand, participants make a sincere effort to understand each other and to clarify what was meant.

Guideline 2 is that IETF participants have impersonal discussions. Ideas are disputed with reasoned argument rather than through intimidation or personal attack. Participants try to provide data and facts for their standpoints so that the rest of the group, who are sitting on the sidelines, can form an opinion. The discussion is easier when the response to a simple question is a polite answer.

Guideline 3 is that IETF participants devise solutions for the global Internet that meet the needs of diverse technical and operational environments. The IETF puts its emphasis on technical competence, rough consensus and individual participation, and it needs to be open to competent input from any source. The document says that "scaling is the ultimate problem" and that many ideas that are quite workable on a small scale fail this crucial test. Participants use their best engineering judgment to find the best solution for the whole Internet, not just the best solution for any particular network, technology, vendor, or user. While everyone has ideas that may stand improvement from time to time, no one shall ever knowingly contribute advice or text that would make a standard technically inferior.

Guideline 4 is that individuals are prepared to contribute to the ongoing work of the group. Participants follow the intellectual property guidelines outlined in BCP 79 and read the relevant Internet-Drafts, RFCs and email archives in order to familiarize themselves with the technology under discussion. Working Group sessions run on a very limited time schedule, and sometimes participants have to limit their questions, because the work of the group continues on the mailing list. Information about a Working Group, including its charter and milestones, is available on the IETF datatracker site or from the Working Group Chair.
sections.plainLanguage: The document lists four guidelines. Treat colleagues with respect, and communicate clearly so that people for whom English is not a first language can follow. Argue about ideas with facts rather than with personal attacks. Design for the whole Internet, not just for one network or vendor. And come prepared, having read the drafts and the mailing list before the meeting.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The IETF guidelines for conduct do not directly affect the security of the Internet. The document does record an expectation that no one shall ever knowingly contribute advice or text that may adversely affect the security of the Internet without describing all known or foreseen risks and threats to potential implementers and users that they are aware of.
sections.plainLanguage: These guidelines do not change how the Internet is secured. The one security expectation is that nobody contributes advice or text that could harm the security of the Internet without first describing the known and foreseen risks.

sections.title: Reporting Transgressions and Consequences
sections.content:
An individual can report transgressions of the guidelines for conduct to the IETF Chair or the IESG.

This document does not discuss measures that can be taken against a participant transgressing the guidelines. Other documents do. RFC 2418 describes a measure where a Working Group Chair has the authority to refuse to grant the floor to any individual who is unprepared or otherwise covering inappropriate material, or who, in the opinion of the Chair, is disrupting the Working Group process. RFC 3683 describes "posting rights" action to remove the posting rights of an individual. RFC 3934 describes a measure through which a Working Group Chair can suspend posting privileges of a disruptive individual for a short period of time.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who breaks the guidelines can be reported to the IETF Chair or the IESG. This document does not say what punishment follows. Other documents let a Working Group Chair refuse the floor, remove posting rights, or suspend posting rights for a short time.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3184
sections.content:
The document lists its changes from RFC 3184. It adds text about the IETF striving to create an environment in which every person is treated with dignity, decency, and respect, and text about contributing advice or text that may affect the security of the Internet.

It removes the recommendation that newcomers should not interfere with the ongoing process in Section 2, because that recommendation can be read as discouraging newcomers from participating in discussions. It replaces the text about the goal of the IETF with text about the mission statement and what the IETF puts its emphasis on, and removes the text about "think globally" because the meaning was not clear. It clarifies the text about English as a first language, and rewords the guideline about impersonal discussions as a positive statement.
sections.plainLanguage: Compared with RFC 3184, this version adds text about dignity and about security, removes the advice that newcomers should stay out of the way, and drops the phrase "think globally" because it was unclear. It also rewrites the impersonal-discussion guideline as a positive statement.

items.title: Respect and courtesy
items.text: Treat colleagues with respect at all times, especially when it is hard to agree.

items.title: Impersonal discussion
items.text: Dispute ideas with reasoned argument and data, not with intimidation or personal attack.

items.title: Global solutions
items.text: Find the best solution for the whole Internet, not for one network, technology, vendor or user.

items.title: Prepared to contribute
items.text: Read the relevant drafts, RFCs and archives, and keep asking questions on the mailing list.
